lessons.title: Study Session 1: Why the Eye Believes What It Sees

blocks.text: Introduction Every flyer, certificate and social media graphic you will ever make in Canva is read before it is understood. A viewer's eye moves across a page in a fraction of a second and decides, before any word is consciously read, whether the page feels organised or confusing. This session teaches you why that happens, so that every design choice you make afterward has a reason behind it rather than a guess.
Learning Outcomes

By the end of this study session, you should be able to: • Explain how the brain groups separate visual elements into a single meaningful pattern. • Identify proximity, similarity, closure and continuity at work in an existing design. • Predict how moving or regrouping elements on a page changes what a viewer perceives as related. • Critique a cluttered or confusing design using the correct perception vocabulary. • Connect visual perception to trust and credibility in her own community or ministry materials.
Main Content
From Confusion to a Reason

Adaeze runs the welfare desk for her church's women's fellowship in Enugu. Every month she posts a flyer for the fellowship meeting, and every month fewer women show up than the group actually has on its register. The flyer is not wrong. It has the date, the time, the venue, a photograph. But it is read as noise, not as an invitation, because nothing on it tells the eye what to look at first, second and third.
What the Eye Does Automatically

In 1923, the German psychologist Max Wertheimer published a study on how the human eye and brain organise what they see. His central finding still holds: the brain does not perceive a page as a collection of separate marks. It automatically groups what it sees into a smaller number of meaningful wholes, and it does this before a person consciously decides to look for a pattern at all. This is the origin of what design teaching now calls the Gestalt principles, from the German word for a unified shape or form.
Four Ways the Eye Groups What It Sees

Proximity Items placed close together are read as belonging to the same group, so on Adaeze's flyer, if the date and the time sit close to each other and far from the venue, a viewer's eye may struggle to connect them as one event. Similarity Items sharing a colour, shape or style are read as related, so repeating the same accent colour on the meeting title and the RSVP line tells the eye they belong together even before the words are read. Closure The brain will complete a shape it can only partly see, which is why a simple broken circle or partial frame can still read clearly as a badge or seal.
Continuity The eye follows a line, a row or a curve, so arranging items along a clear line guides the eye through a page in the order intended rather than in a scattered path.
Key Practices

• Proximity: group related items close together. • Similarity: repeat colour, shape or style to signal relationship. • Closure: trust the eye to complete a simple, partly shown shape. • Continuity: arrange items along a line to guide the eye's path.
A Worked Example: Two Versions of One Flyer

Picture Adaeze's original fellowship flyer: the meeting title in small text at the top, a large decorative border taking up a third of the page, the date buried in a paragraph of welcome text, and the venue printed in the same size as everything else. A viewer's eye has nowhere obvious to land, so it lands nowhere in particular, and the flyer is skimmed rather than read. Now picture a redesigned version. The meeting title is the largest text on the page, using contrast to claim first attention. The date, time and venue sit close together in their own block, using proximity to read as one connected detail. The decorative border is replaced with a single accent colour repeated in the title and the RSVP line, using similarity to tie the page together. Nothing about the content changed. Only the grouping did. This is the actual test of Session 1: not whether a design looks pretty, but whether a stranger who has never seen the flyer before can tell, in under three seconds, what it wants her to know and do.
Common Pitfalls

A beginner who has just learned these four principles often overcorrects, adding heavy borders or bold colour to every single element at once in an attempt to make everything stand out. When everything is emphasised, nothing is, and the page returns to the same unreadable noise it started as. Apply grouping and emphasis to the one or two things that genuinely need it, and let everything else stay quiet in support.
What This Frees You From

None of this asks Adaeze to become an artist. It asks her to notice, before she opens Canva, which piece of information a viewer should see first, and to use grouping, closeness and repeated colour to put that information where the eye will actually land first. A flyer built this way does not need more decoration. It needs a clearer shape.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned that a viewer's eye automatically groups what it sees through proximity, similarity, closure and continuity, and you practised naming these patterns in a real flyer. This prepares you for Study Session 2, where you will build hands-on fluency with the Canva workspace itself.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Which of the four grouping principles is a flyer you have seen recently using well, and which is it missing? 2. Think of a piece of information you once missed on a form or notice because it was placed too far from related information. What would you change about its layout now? Practical Output: Practical Output A four-part review of one existing flyer, naming exactly where proximity, similarity, closure and continuity are working or missing on it.
References and Further Reading

• Wertheimer, M. (1923). Foundational study on the laws of perceptual organisation, widely credited as the origin of the Gestalt principles of proximity, similarity, closure and continuity used throughout design practice today.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 2: Getting to Know Canva

blocks.text: Introduction This session is your walk through the room before you start building anything in it. You will learn where the tools live, how a Canva design is structured, and how to move around confidently before you are asked to make design decisions.
Learning Outcomes

By the end of this study session, you should be able to: • Navigate the Canva workspace, including templates, elements, uploads and text tools. • Create and correctly resize a design canvas for a specific stated purpose. • Use layers, grouping and alignment tools to organise elements on a page. • Save and export a finished design in the file format suited to its intended use.
Main Content
A Room Worth Walking Through Slowly

Fatoumata coordinates activity sheets for children at a community resettlement programme in Bamako, and until recently she designed every notice by hand with a ruler and coloured pencils before a volunteer typed it up separately. Her first afternoon in Canva felt like walking into a large workshop with every tool already laid out, more overwhelming than the pencils had been, simply because there was so much visible at once. This session exists because that first afternoon is where most beginners either build confidence or quietly give up.
Canvas, Layers and Panels

A Canva design begins with a canvas size, and the size should match where the design will actually be seen. A WhatsApp flyer, an Instagram post and a printed A4 notice are not the same shape, and starting with the correct size saves the redesign that happens when the wrong shape is stretched or cropped later. Inside that canvas, everything you place, whether a photograph, a shape, a line of text or a sticker, sits on its own layer, stacked like sheets of paper. Understanding layers explains why a text box sometimes disappears behind an image, and the fix is almost always to bring that layer forward rather than to delete and start again.

2.2b Templates as a Starting Point, Not a Finish Line Canva's ready-made templates are useful for structure and speed, especially in a learner's first weeks, but a template should be treated as scaffolding rather than a finished product. Changing the colours, the fonts and the arrangement of a template to fit your own purpose, rather than only swapping in your own text, is what turns a borrowed layout into an original design that actually reflects the message you are sending.
Three Practices for Moving Confidently in Canva

Finding the Right Panel The Elements panel holds shapes, icons, lines and frames; the Uploads panel holds your own photographs; the Text panel holds ready-made heading and body styles as a starting point, not a fixed rule. Aligning and Grouping On Purpose

Selecting two or more objects at once and using Canva's align tools will centre or evenly space them far more reliably than moving them by eye, which matters once you reach the composition principles in Session 3. Grouping related objects together, for example a name and a small icon beside it, means they move as one piece rather than drifting apart while you edit. Exporting for the Right Screen A design meant to be printed needs a higher resolution PNG or PDF; a design meant to be shared on a phone screen needs a smaller, web-optimised file.
Key Practices

• Match canvas size to where the design will actually be seen. • Use layers deliberately, bringing hidden elements forward rather than restarting. • Align and group related objects instead of positioning by eye. • Export the file format suited to print or to screen, on purpose.
Beyond the Basics: Brand Kit, Resize and Sharing

Once the core workspace feels familiar, three further Canva features are worth knowing early, even before they are needed. Brand Kit lets you save a business or ministry's colours and fonts once, so every future design pulls from the same saved palette instead of being rebuilt from memory each time, which is where the repetition principle from Session 3 becomes automatic rather than effortful. Magic Resize takes a finished design and reshapes it for a different platform, turning a printed A4 flyer into a correctly proportioned Instagram post without rebuilding it from scratch, though the result should always be checked afterward since text that fit one shape does not always sit as cleanly in another. Sharing and collaboration tools allow a design to be sent to a facilitator or mentor for comment directly inside Canva, with comments attached to the exact part of the design being discussed, rather than trying to describe a change over a voice note or a screenshot.
Common Pitfalls

Two habits slow beginners down more than any missing tool. The first is browsing templates for inspiration before deciding what the design needs to say, which usually produces a design shaped by someone else's content rather than the learner's own. The second is exporting immediately after finishing, without checking the design at actual size on a phone screen first, where a headline that looked fine on a laptop can turn out cramped or too small to read.
Designing on Purpose

Fatoumata's resettlement notices now go out correctly sized for the noticeboard and, separately, correctly sized for the WhatsApp groups families actually check first, because she learned to export each version on purpose rather than by accident.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to move confidently through the Canva workspace: choosing the right canvas size, working with layers, aligning and grouping objects, and exporting for the right screen. This prepares you for Study Session 3, where you will apply a practical checklist to strengthen any design.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment

1. Which part of the Canva workspace felt least familiar the first time you opened it, and what helped it make sense? 2. Describe, in your own words, the difference between a layer and a canvas. Practical Output: Practical Output One new Canva design, sized for a WhatsApp flyer, with a grouped heading and body text, exported as a PNG.
References and Further Reading
This study session covers Canva tool literacy, a practical skill rather than a research claim, so no external citation is used here.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 3: The Four Principles of Strong Design

blocks.text: Introduction Session 1 explained why the eye organises what it sees. This session gives you a practical checklist you can apply to almost any design, so that once you know what to look for, a cluttered page becomes an obvious, fixable problem rather than a vague feeling that something is wrong.
Learning Outcomes

By the end of this study session, you should be able to: • Define contrast, repetition, alignment and proximity as design principles. • Locate each of the four principles at work in an existing design, both where it succeeds and where it fails. • Apply all four principles to correct a cluttered flyer. • Explain why repetition builds trust and recognition across a set of related materials. • Self-assess a design draft against the four principles before calling it finished.
Main Content
A Checklist, Not a Feeling

Precious designs invoices and receipts for the small tailoring business she runs from home in Port Harcourt, most of it typed on her phone in the short windows while her baby naps. Her early invoices looked busy without her understanding why, until a mentor showed her a simple checklist: contrast, repetition, alignment, proximity.
The CRAP Principles

In 1994, the designer Robin Williams published The Non-Designer's Design Book, built around exactly these four principles, remembered by the acronym CRAP. Contrast means that different elements should look clearly different, through size, weight, or colour, so that the most important item on a page is unmistakably the most important one; a heading in the same size and colour as the body text gives the eye nothing to land on first. Repetition means that a design's visual choices, a colour, a font, a line style, should repeat consistently across a page and across a whole set of materials, which is what makes a business's invoices, flyers and receipts feel like they come from the same hand even when a client has never seen the business name before.
Applying the Four Principles

Contrast The most important item on the page should be unmistakably the most important one, through size, weight or colour, not left to blend in with everything around it. Repetition A design's colours, fonts and line styles should repeat consistently, not just within one page but across a whole set of materials from the same source. Alignment Every element should connect to an invisible line shared with something else on the page, rather than sitting wherever it happens to have been typed.
Proximity Related items are grouped close together, and unrelated items are given clear space apart, so grouping itself becomes part of how the information is read.
Key Practices

• Make the most important item unmistakably the most important one. • Repeat colours, fonts and styles across a full set of materials. • Align every element to a shared line rather than placing it by feel. • Group related items and separate unrelated ones.
A Worked Example: Precious's Invoice, Before and After

Precious's early invoice had a business name in playful script, a total due in the same weight as the line items above it, dates that were sometimes centred and sometimes left-aligned depending on her mood that day, and a thank-you note pressed right up against the payment details with no space between them. Running it through the four questions changed very little of the content and almost everything about how it read. Contrast: the total due became bold and noticeably larger than every other figure. Repetition: the same accent colour and script-free heading font now appear on every invoice she sends. Alignment: every date, every figure and every label now sits on the same left edge. Proximity: the thank-you note moved down, with clear space separating it from the payment details it used to crowd. A client paying that invoice today does not consciously notice any of these four decisions. She simply finds the amount owed immediately, which is the entire point.
Common Pitfalls

The most common mistake at this stage is applying only one of the four principles and assuming the design is finished. A flyer can have excellent contrast and still fail on alignment, or excellent repetition across a business's materials and still fail on proximity within a single page. All four should be checked every time, not just the one that comes most naturally.
A Question Before Sending

Precious now runs every invoice through the same four questions before sending it: is the most important number the most visually obvious one, does it use the same colours and fonts as her last invoice, are the lines actually aligned to each other, and are related figures grouped with clear space around unrelated ones. The invoices did not become more decorated. They became easier to trust at a glance, which for a small business asking to be paid on time matters more than decoration ever could.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned the four CRAP principles, contrast, repetition, alignment and proximity, and practised checking a design against all four before calling it finished. This prepares you for Study Session 4, where you will apply the same discipline to typography.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Look at a receipt, flyer or certificate you have received recently. Which of the four principles does it use well, and which one is weakest?

2. If you had to fix only one of the four principles on a cluttered design, which would you choose first, and why? Practical Output: Practical Output A redesign of the Session 1 flyer applying all four principles, with one sentence naming the single biggest change made.
References and Further Reading

• Williams, R. (1994). The Non-Designer's Design Book, the source of the CRAP principles of contrast, repetition, alignment and proximity now widely taught as the foundation of applied graphic design.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

modules.title: Part 2
modules.overview: Canva Graphic Design and Visual Communication — Part 2. Study each session, complete the reflection and practical output, and pass the part quiz before moving forward.

blocks.text: Introduction The words on a page are read through their shape long before they are read for their meaning. This session teaches you to choose and arrange text so that it is read easily and in the right order, by anyone, including a reader whose eyesight is not perfect.
Learning Outcomes

By the end of this study session, you should be able to: • Distinguish common typeface categories and describe when each is appropriate to use. • Explain visual hierarchy through size, weight and spacing. • Pair two typefaces in a single design without visual conflict. • Apply hierarchy correctly to a real document, such as a flyer or a one-page notice.
Main Content
A Beautiful Font That Fails Its Job

Naledi lives with low vision and runs a small stationery shop in Gaborone. She reads most screens at a larger zoom than her friends do, and she is quick to notice when a designer has chosen a delicate, thin font for an important announcement simply because it looked elegant on a laptop screen. Her honest feedback, given to a friend designing a community notice, is where this session begins: a beautiful font that cannot be read quickly by a real reader has failed at its only job.
Hierarchy and Rhythm

In 1992, the typographer Robert Bringhurst published The Elements of Typographic Style, still treated as one of the standard references on how text should be shaped and arranged on a page. Bringhurst's central concern is hierarchy and rhythm, the idea that a page of text should guide a reader's eye through it in a deliberate order, from the most important line to the least, using size, weight and spacing rather than colour or decoration alone. A heading does not need to be flamboyant to do its job. It needs to be unmistakably larger, or bolder, or both, than the text beneath it, and that difference needs to be consistent across every page of the same document.
Choosing and Pairing Type

Knowing the Families Serif faces, with small finishing strokes at the ends of letters, read as more formal or traditional in print; sans- serif faces, without those strokes, read as cleaner and are usually easier to read on a small phone screen; script and decorative faces imitate handwriting or add flourish, and are almost never suitable for body text because they slow a reader down. Pairing With Purpose A common and reliable pairing is one sans-serif for headings and a second, different sans-serif or a simple serif for body text, chosen so the two are clearly different in style rather than nearly identical, which reads as a mistake rather than a choice. Size and Contrast as Access

A heading set too small, or body text set in pale grey on a white background, is not merely a style preference; it can make a design genuinely unreadable to someone with low vision, an older reader, or anyone reading in bright sunlight on a phone.
Key Practices

• Choose typeface families that suit the reading context, not only the mood. • Pair two clearly different typefaces rather than two nearly identical ones. • Set a heading unmistakably larger or bolder than body text, consistently. • Treat size and contrast as access, not decoration.
Spacing, Line Length and Legibility

Choosing the right typeface is only half of typography. How that typeface is spaced matters just as much. Line spacing, sometimes called leading, that is too tight crowds each line into the one below it and tires a reader quickly; spacing that is too loose makes a paragraph feel disconnected, as though each line belongs to a different thought. A comfortable middle ground, generally a little more than the height of the letters themselves, keeps a paragraph easy to follow. Line length matters in the same way. A line of body text stretched across an entire wide flyer forces a reader's eye to travel a long way and then hunt for the start of the next line, while a line that is too narrow breaks a thought awkwardly every few words. Body text is usually easiest to read in a moderate column width, not the full page. One further habit is worth naming directly: setting an entire heading, let alone a full paragraph, in capital letters removes the natural rise and fall of letter shapes that a reader's eye actually uses to recognise words quickly, and should be used sparingly, for a short label or a single word of emphasis, not for a full sentence.
Common Pitfalls

A frequent error is choosing a typeface for its personality rather than its legibility, especially for headings meant to grab attention. A striking, unusual typeface can work well for a single short word, but the same typeface used for a full sentence or a paragraph almost always slows the reader down, however striking it looked in the font list.
Access, Not Decoration
For Naledi and for every reader like her, size and contrast are not decoration, they are access. The next session on colour returns to this exact point with a specific, checkable standard.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to choose and pair typefaces with visual hierarchy, and to treat readable size and contrast as a matter of access rather than decoration. This prepares you for Study Session 5, where colour receives the same accessible, purposeful treatment.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Find a design, printed or digital, where you struggled to tell what to read first. What typographic choice caused that confusion? 2. Naledi's feedback focused on readability over decoration. Where in your own designs might you be choosing decoration over readability without realising it? Practical Output: Practical Output The Session 3 flyer with clear typographic hierarchy applied, naming the two paired typefaces used and why.
References and Further Reading
• Bringhurst, R. (1992). The Elements of Typographic Style. Point Roberts, WA: Hartley & Marks Publishers.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

Introduction Colour is the fastest thing a viewer notices on any design, faster than the words, faster than the layout. This session teaches you to choose colour with intention, and to check that your choices are actually readable, not only attractive.
Learning Outcomes

By the end of this study session, you should be able to: • Use the colour wheel to build complementary, analogous and triadic palettes. • Explain the psychological effect of warm colour compared with cool colour in a design. • Apply the minimum accessible contrast standard for readable text against a background. • Choose a three-colour palette suited to a defined audience and purpose. • Identify low-contrast failures in an existing design.
Main Content
A Correction Worth Receiving

Chiamaka began designing wedding invitations and memorial programmes from her home in Owerri after her husband passed, turning a skill she had once used only for church programmes into a small, steady income. Her early designs used colours she personally loved, without asking whether those colours suited a grieving family's memorial programme or a joyful couple's invitation, and a client's gentle correction taught her that colour carries meaning whether or not the designer intends it to.
The Colour Wheel

In 1961, the artist and Bauhaus teacher Johannes Itten published The Art of Color, still one of the standard references on how colour relates to itself on the wheel. Itten's twelve-part colour wheel organises red, yellow and blue as primary colours, with the colours between them mixed from those three. From that wheel, three reliable palette structures follow: complementary colours sit directly opposite each other and create the strongest possible contrast, useful for a single bold accent; analogous colours sit beside each other and create a calm, harmonious feeling, suited to something gentle like a memorial programme; triadic colours sit at three evenly spaced points and create a lively, balanced palette, suited to something celebratory like a wedding or a children's programme.
Choosing Colour on Purpose

Warm and Cool Warm colours, reds, oranges and yellows, tend to feel energetic, urgent or celebratory, while cool colours, blues, greens and purples, tend to feel calm, trustworthy or reflective. Neither is correct on its own; the choice depends entirely on what the design is for. Choosing a Palette Structure Chiamaka now asks one question before opening her colour palette: is this design meant to feel urgent and joyful, or calm and steady, and she chooses a complementary, analogous or triadic structure accordingly. Checking Accessible Contrast

The World Wide Web Consortium's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, published in their 2.1 revision in 2018, set a minimum readable contrast ratio of 4.5 to 1 between ordinary body text and its background. A soft grey text on a white background often looks elegant on a bright laptop screen and fails this standard completely on an older phone in daylight, exactly the situation Naledi described in Session 4.
Key Practices

• Match warm or cool tone to what the design needs to feel like. • Choose complementary, analogous or triadic structure on purpose. • Check body text against the 4.5 to 1 minimum contrast standard. • Treat beauty and readability as two separate, equally necessary tests.
Designing for Colour Blindness

Accessible colour is not only about contrast against a background. A meaningful number of viewers, most commonly men, experience some form of colour blindness, most often difficulty distinguishing red from green. A chart, a status label or an instruction that relies only on colour, for example red text for a warning with no other visual signal, can become genuinely unreadable to a viewer who cannot reliably tell that colour apart from a neighbouring one. The fix is straightforward once it is known: never let colour alone carry the full meaning. Pair a colour choice with a second signal, a label, an icon, a pattern or a difference in shape, so the information still comes through even for a viewer who perceives the colours differently than intended. Chiamaka now applies this directly to her memorial programmes, where a printed order of service sometimes uses colour to separate sections; she pairs each colour change with a clear heading rather than relying on the colour shift alone to signal a new section.
Common Pitfalls

A common mistake is choosing colours in isolation, one at a time, rather than testing the full palette together against the design's actual background. A colour that reads clearly on white can disappear entirely against a photograph or a tinted background, so the full combination should always be checked in the finished design, not only in the colour picker.
Beauty Is Not the Only Test

Beauty is not the only test a colour choice must pass. Checking a colour pairing against the accessible contrast standard before finishing a design is now part of Chiamaka's process, not an afterthought.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to build a colour palette on purpose using the colour wheel, and to check it against the WCAG minimum contrast standard rather than relying on appearance alone. This prepares you for Study Session 6, where every session's teaching comes together in one finished design.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Choose a design you have made or seen recently. Was its colour palette complementary, analogous or triadic, and did that choice suit its purpose? 2. Check a design of your own against the 4.5 to 1 contrast standard, using an online contrast checker if one is available to you. What did you find? Practical Output: Practical Output A three-colour palette built for a chosen purpose, applied to the Session 4 design and confirmed against the 4.5 to 1 contrast standard.
References and Further Reading
• Itten, J. (1961). The Art of Color. • World Wide Web Consortium (2018). Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

Introduction Every session so far has taught one part of the whole. This final session asks you to plan a real design brief from a real request and build one complete piece in Canva that uses everything you now know, from perception through to accessible colour.
Learning Outcomes

By the end of this study session, you should be able to: • Plan a design brief from a real request, identifying purpose, audience and the single most important piece of information. • Apply perception, the four core principles, typography and colour together in one finished Canva design. • Give and receive peer feedback using the vocabulary built across Sessions 1 to 5. • Finish and export one complete design as evidence of learning.
Main Content
The Question That Changes Everything

Imani teaches Saturday computer classes to teenage girls at a community centre in Dar es Salaam, and her own turning point in this pathway came when a fellow learner asked her, plainly, what a flyer she had made was actually for. She realised she had opened Canva and started dragging elements onto the page before deciding what the single most important piece of information was. Every session in this course has been building toward avoiding exactly that mistake.
A Design Brief in Three Questions

A design brief, even an informal one written for yourself, answers three questions before you touch Canva: who is this for, what is the one thing they must walk away knowing, and where will they see it, a phone screen, a printed noticeboard, or both. Answering these first turns a blank canvas from something intimidating into something you already know how to fill, because every choice that follows, canvas size, hierarchy, colour, has a clear reason behind it.
Applying Five Sessions in Order

Grouping (Session 1) A viewer's eye naturally clusters what sits nearby and separates what sits apart, so keep related items near each other and give unrelated items room. Before placing a single element, decide which two or three pieces of information belong together, and let that decision guide the whole layout. The Four Principles (Session 3) Run the finished draft against contrast, repetition, alignment and proximity as a checklist, deliberately, before calling it done. This is the fastest way to catch a design that looks acceptable at a glance but would not survive a closer look. Hierarchy (Session 4)

Set one unmistakably dominant line so a reader always knows where to look first, and make sure the typefaces chosen for that hierarchy are paired deliberately rather than left to whatever Canva suggests by default. Colour (Session 5) Choose a palette on purpose, matching warm or cool tone to what the design needs to feel like, and confirm it against the accessible contrast standard before the design is considered finished, not after.
Key Practices

• Write a three-question brief before opening Canva. • Group related information and separate unrelated information. • Check the draft against contrast, repetition, alignment and proximity. • Confirm hierarchy and colour before exporting.
Giving and Receiving Feedback Well

A Learning Circle works best when feedback uses the vocabulary this course has built rather than a vague reaction. Saying a design feels busy is far less useful than saying it needs clearer proximity, or that its heading is not contrasting enough against the body text. Naming the specific principle turns a feeling into something the designer can actually act on. Receiving feedback well matters just as much as giving it. A design is not the designer, so a note about weak contrast or a cluttered layout is a comment about the page, not a judgement of the woman who made it. Imani's own turning point in this course came from exactly this kind of specific, respectful question asked by a fellow learner, not from criticism aimed at her personally. Before this course closes, consider offering one piece of principle-based feedback to another learner's Session 6 design, and receiving one in return, using the same vocabulary this course has spent six sessions building together.
Common Pitfalls

The most common mistake at the capstone stage is rushing straight to Canva out of excitement to finish, skipping the three-question brief that Session 6 opened with. A design built without a brief usually still looks acceptable, but it is far harder to explain afterward why any particular choice was made, which is the actual skill this course has been building.
A Habit, Not a Portfolio

Imani's finished flyer for her next computer class was, by her own account, not dramatically different from her earlier ones in decoration. It was different in that every choice on the page could be explained if someone asked her why. That is the actual outcome of this course: not a portfolio of pretty designs, though those will come with Course 80 later in this pathway, but the habit of designing on purpose, session after session, design after design.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to plan a short design brief and apply perception, the four core principles, typography and colour together in one complete Canva design. This closes Course 76 and prepares you for Course 77, Social Media Visual Design.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment

1. Write your own three-question design brief (who is it for, what must they know, where will they see it) for a real notice, flyer or invitation you need to make soon. 2. Looking back across all six sessions, which single principle changed your designing the most, and why? Practical Output: Practical Output One complete Canva design built from a real request, exported, with a two to three sentence explanation of the layout, typography and colour choices behind it.
